title: Stochastic fair sampling window scheduler proposal
content:
Purpose:
This is a working proposal for a stochastic, windowed sampling scheduler for continuous batching in the serving runtime. It aims to balance latency-sensitive request-level fairness with token-level efficiency and KV cache locality by probabilistically grouping tokens into scheduling windows rather than using strict deterministic time or size thresholds.

Why a new approach:
- We need an approach that degrades gracefully across a wide distribution of request shapes (short chat turns, long generations, high-concurrency low-QPS tenants).
- Existing deterministic windows (fixed micro-windows or pure request-level queues) either — in practice — starve long requests (when we prefer request-level fairness) or waste latency headroom (when we aggressively wait for tokens to form large batches).
- Kernel performance is highly nonlinear in batch shape and KV locality; small improvements in coalescing often give outsized throughput gains but can introduce tail latency spikes for under-served clients.

Core idea (intuitive):
- Maintain a continuous token-stream buffer per backend worker. Rather than slicing the buffer strictly by time or by request, we maintain overlapping stochastic windows: each incoming token decides with a small randomized probability p whether to start/extend a sampling window. Windows collect tokens for a short adaptive horizon (H) and submit them as one batch to the inference kernel.
- The randomness prevents long-lived priority inversions and reduces pathological synchronization across clients (avoids burst collisions).
- Windows include lightweight metadata: originating request id, cumulative token-length, kv-cache-affinity-hint (hash of the key-set), and a priority score computed from SLA, client weight, and token-age.

Design constraints and invariants:
- Request-level fairness: no request should be starved indeﬁnitely. We enforce this by attaching a token-age watermark per request; if any token from a request exceeds age threshold A, that token is prioritized into the next window submission (forced inclusion).
- KV-cache locality: attempt to co-locate tokens that share KV-affinity hints into the same window to maximize KV hits and reduce memory churn. Affinity is treated as a soft factor in window selection (higher weight increases likelihood of inclusion).
- Kernel-friendly shapes: windows should prefer shapes that the selected kernel handles well (e.g., many short requests vs one long request). The window scoring function includes a kernel-shape score learned from past kernel latency/tflops traces.
- Latency SLO guardrails: windows cannot delay tokens past a strict upper bound (hard SLO boundary).

Algorithm (high-level pseudocode):
- On token arrival (t):
  - compute token_metadata = {req_id, token_len, kv_hint, priority_base, arrival_ts}
  - with probability p(req_id, system_load, token_age) mark token as "window-starter"
  - place token in per-worker waiting set W
  - if token_marked_starter then create or extend window:
      window.expiry = now + H(adaptive)
      window.tokens += token
      window.score = recompute(window)
  - periodically (every microtick) evaluate open windows:
      - if now >= window.expiry or window.score >= submit_threshold or any token.age >= A then submit(window)
      - otherwise maybe merge compatible windows with high kv-affinity and compatible kernel-shape scoring

Scoring function components (linear combination):
- fairness_score = function(min_token_age_in_window, max_token_age_in_window, per-req-priority)
- kv_affinity_score = normalized sum of pairwise kv_hint matches
- kernel_shape_score = predicted kernel throughput uplift if these tokens are batched
- size_penalty = negative term for windows that create too skewed request-level shapes
- randomness_boost = small additive term to maintain stochasticity

Adaptive components:
- p (starter probability) decays with worker load and increases for older tokens/requests. This keeps more windows from starting under high load while guaranteeing eventual inclusion.
- H (window horizon) shortens if median latency approaches SLO; lengthens when worker utilization is low and kernels perform better with bigger batches.
- submit_threshold is tuned per-model and per-kernel; default derives from offline kernel profiling data.

KV cache notes:
- Every window computes a kv_merge_plan: order tokens by estimated KV key reuse. The runtime will attempt to build a single KV prefix and assign tokens appropriate offsets to maximize in-kernel cache hits.
- For tokens that reference large disjoint key sets, the scheduler prefers splitting into multiple windows to avoid polluting kernel-local cache. The kv_affinity_score helps surface this.

Fairness guarantees (soft + hard):
- Soft: weighted fairness across clients implemented via priority_base and fairness_score. Over time, proportion of service matches configured client weights with high probability due to randomized starts and age-based boosts.
- Hard: token-age cap A guarantees bounded waiting time for any token, preventing starvation. A is tuned to be <= 90th percentile latency SLO for the tenant when under typical load.

Interaction with request-level semantics:
- We maintain per-request completion callbacks; windows submit tokens and the runtime assembles responses to appropriate request streams. For streaming responses we ensure partial flushes are possible when a window includes early-turn tokens.
- For function-calling or structural output, the scheduler ensures request-level ordering by prioritizing tokens from the same logical request into the same window where practical. If splitting is unavoidable, reassembly happens in the worker and ordering metadata is preserved.

Kernel selection and feedback loop:
- Each completed window provides telemetry: observed latency, kernel utilization, kv_hit_rate, and per-request tail percentiles. A lightweight online learner updates kernel_shape_score and submit_threshold estimates per model/kernels pair.
- If a kernel consistently underperforms for particular shapes, the scheduler reduces kernel_shape_score for similar windows and routes them to alternate kernels or splits them.

Metrics & experiment plan:
- Primary metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (token and request-complete), tokens/sec per-GPU, kernel utilization, KV cache hit rate, per-tenant fairness ratio (observed service vs configured weight).
- Secondary: request reassembly overhead, memory churn in kernel, variance of batch shapes.
- A/B experiment: rollout to 10% of workers for 2 weeks with traffic sampling across tenants (mix short chat vs long generation). Monitor regressions in p99 tail (>5% relative) and throughput delta (>3% improvement target).
- Canary triggers: if tail latency worsens by >10% for any top-20 tenant, rollback and capture trace.

Implementation notes and APIs: 
- Configuration knobs (operator settable): base_p, A(token_age_cap), H_base, min_window_size, submit_threshold, kernel_profile_id. These are persisted as per-cluster config with per-model overrides.
- Data structures: lightweight window descriptor (linked list of token refs), per-worker waiting set (heap keyed by window.score), per-request watermark tracker. Keep descriptors O(1) memory per token reference.
- Backpressure: if kernel queue length exceeds queue_limit, the starter probability p is decayed aggressively and windows shift to smaller H to reduce queueing pressure.

Open questions and tradeoffs: 
- Choosing p: what is the right mapping from load/age to starter probability to avoid thundering herd? Need sims.
- Merge policy: heuristics for merging windows with complementary KV hints need microbenchmarks; naive merging can hurt kernel shapes.
- Kernel learning cold-start: how quickly can online learner adapt without destabilizing scheduling decisions? Add exploration schedule.
- Cross-worker coordination: do we coordinate kv-affinity across workers to avoid duplicate KV builds? Coordination increases complexity and latency; evaluate harvesting affinity within worker only vs global.

Experiment checklist (short-term):
- Build simulator that takes historical request traces and kernel profiles -> run stochastic-window algorithm to predict throughput/latency tradeoffs.
- Implement prototype in one worker process with diagnostics and a /debug endpoint to visualize window compositions in real-time.
- Instrument kernel to report kv_hit_rate and batch shapings per-window.
- Run canary with 5 tenants: two chatty low-latency tenants, two batch-generation tenants, one mixed. Observe fairness ratios.

Notes to self (todo):
- Write the simulator harness (trace ingestion + kernel-profile loader).
- Draft RFC for operators about new tuning knobs and safe defaults.
- Add unit test for age-based forced-inclusion path.
- Gather kernel profile histograms from last 30 days for models: redwood-7b-instruct, open-ml-13b, quant-4/8 variants.

- past continuous batching experiments: file://../continuous-batcher-design-notes-token-level-vs-request-level.json (see sims section)
- related: per-client-sla-priority-batcher-proposal.json, request-token-bridge-heuristics-chronicle.json

End of draft.
